data.title: Same Tree
data.summary:
Input: Two binary trees p and q.
Output: A boolean indicating whether the two trees are structurally identical and have the same node values.
Rules: The structure and node values must match exactly.
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100].

data.key_insight: Two trees are identical if and only if their root values are equal, their left subtrees are identical, and their right subtrees are identical.

steps.title: Base Cases
steps.detail: If both nodes p and q are None, return True since they are identical empty subtrees.

steps.title: Structural Mismatch Check
steps.detail: If one of the nodes is None while the other is not, return False because the structures do not match.

steps.title: Value Mismatch Check
steps.detail: If the values of nodes p and q are different, return False.

steps.title: Recursive Traversal
steps.detail: Recursively check if the left subtrees are identical and the right subtrees are identical, returning the logical AND of both results.

data.pattern_summary: Depth-First Search explores a tree by going as deep as possible down each branch before backtracking. Reach for it when you need to process hierarchical data or compare tree structures recursively.

pattern_options.name: Depth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Comparing two trees node by node naturally maps to traversing both simultaneously using recursion.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are designed for linear structures like arrays or strings, not branching tree nodes.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps store frequencies or key-value pairs, but tree comparisons depend heavily on exact parent-child positions and structure.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays or sublists, which does not apply to hierarchical trees.

signals.phrase: Two binary trees p and q
signals.hint: Indicates you are working with hierarchical node structures instead of flat sequences.

signals.phrase: structurally identical and have the same node values
signals.hint: Means every single corresponding node position and value must be checked between both inputs.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach serializes each binary tree completely into a list representation using a level-order traversal, and then compares the two resulting lists for exact equality.
data.brute_force_why: It visits every single node in both trees multiple times to build and clean up the list representations.
data.bottleneck: Converting the entire trees into separate lists before comparing requires storing all values in memory and traversing the structures multiple times unnecessarily.
bottleneck_hints: Do you actually need to convert the entire tree into a list before checking if it matches?
Think about whether you can check the current nodes and immediately recurse instead of waiting until the end.
What if you compared the root values and subtrees on the fly during a single traversal?

data.overview: The algorithm checks if two binary trees are identical by recursively comparing their current nodes and subtrees. It returns true only if both trees have matching structure and identical node values at every corresponding position.
data.intuition: Imagine comparing two family trees side by side by holding hands with your twin and checking every relative, starting from the oldest ancestor down to the youngest, ensuring every single branch matches.

data.insight: Instead of flattening trees into lists and comparing them entirely, the recursive approach compares both trees node by node simultaneously. It halts and returns false immediately upon hitting a structural mismatch or differing value, avoiding unnecessary work.

derivation.note: Executes once for every node in the smaller tree to check for null boundaries.
Executes to verify if only one of the nodes is null.
Executes to compare the values of non-null nodes.
Recursively visits both left and right children, scaling linearly with the number of nodes.

data.time_summary: Summing the costs across all lines yields O(N) time complexity, where N is the number of nodes in the smaller tree, because every node is visited at most once.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(H) where H is the height of the tree, consumed by the call stack during recursive traversal.
data.takeaway: When comparing two tree structures, traverse them simultaneously and short-circuit at the first difference rather than flattening them first.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if both nodes are null before checking if only one is null.
Comparing flattened tree arrays which fails when null children are omitted or incorrectly placed.
Returning true when one tree ends before the other.
